analysis.one_liner: Extended wage, benefit, safety, and union protections to part-time, temporary, and misclassified workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or floor vote; it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal labor law to cover the growing part-time, temporary, and contract workforce. It would have raised the minimum wage in steps to $6.75 by 1998 and indexed it to average wages, required equal pay for part-time and temporary workers doing the same work as full-timers, extended anti-discrimination and workplace safety laws to independent contractors, let temps and part-timers join union bargaining units, required notice of layoffs to part-time employees, and given workers on expiring federal service contracts first shot at the successor contractor's jobs. It also would have expanded family and medical leave, pension and health benefits, and unemployment insurance to contingent workers, and barred companies that willfully misclassify employees as independent contractors from winning federal or defense contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time, temporary, leased, and contract workers who currently earn less than full-timers doing the same work and often lack health, pension, and unemployment coverage. Also taxpayers, who effectively subsidize employers that shift payroll taxes onto workers via misclassification, and honest competing contractors.

how_it_helps.text: Raised the minimum wage in annual steps to $6.75 by 1998 and tied it thereafter to half of average hourly earnings, so it would rise with wages rather than eroding with inflation.
Required equal pay for part-time and temporary workers doing the same work as full-time employees, with exceptions only for seniority, merit, production systems, or other non-status factors.
Extended civil rights protections against religion, sex, national origin, age, and disability discrimination to independent contractors, who were previously outside those laws.

Extended family and medical leave to workers with as little as 125 hours of service over three months, instead of the 1,250 hours over twelve months the law required, and required group health plans to give part-time workers a proportional employer premium contribution.

Gave part-time and temporary workers with reasonable expectations of continued employment the right to be included in union bargaining units, and required employers to protect temporary workers on their premises from safety hazards.

Required states to let part-time workers collect unemployment insurance and made companies that willfully misclassified employees as independent contractors ineligible for federal contracts for two years.

Gave workers on expiring federal service contracts a right of first refusal on jobs under the successor contractor, ending the routine practice of replacing the whole workforce at contract turnover to shed wages and benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on lower-paid contingent labor to cut costs — particularly temp agencies, federal contractors, and large users of part-time staff — plus some administrative burden on pension and health plans.

drawbacks.text: The wage schedule raised the federal minimum from $4.25 to $6.75 by 1998, a large jump for small businesses and labor-intensive industries, some of which would respond by cutting jobs or hours rather than absorbing the cost.

The bill's broad mandates — equal pay for part-timers, group health coverage for anyone working under 30 hours, pension counting for 500-hour workers, and deeming contractors' workers to be joint employees — would have significantly raised the cost of using temporary and part-time labor, which critics argued could lead employers to reduce contingent hiring rather than upgrade the jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for workers were substantial and broad: higher wages, equal pay for part-timers, health and pension access, unemployment coverage, and protection from misclassification. The costs fell on employers who used contingent labor to cut costs, plus some administrative burden on pension and health plan administrators. The main design risk was cost-shifting — firms could respond to the higher wage floor and benefit mandates by cutting hours or headcount, and the bill's equal-pay mandate for temp and part-time workers could have made some employers reluctant to hire contingent workers at all. On balance it was a well-aimed bill whose main flaw was scale: it attacked a labor-market trend all at once rather than phasing in.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and never went anywhere — no hearing, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 5, 1994, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No further action was ever taken; the record shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who relied on cheaper contingent labor, and firms that misclassified workers to avoid payroll taxes and benefits, kept the status quo.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Business and temporary-staffing industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending wage, benefit, and collective bargaining protections to contingent workers; a measure of their influence is that a Senate controlled by the same party as the sponsor never took up the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the referred bill — no hearings or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, only one other Democrat signed on, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill died in committee without any vote.

industries.note: The bill targeted the business model of supplying cheaper, unprotected contingent labor: equal pay for equal work, joint-employer status, safety duties, and successor-employee rights on federal contracts would all squeeze margins. Their interest ran against the workers the bill covered.

Would have faced debarment for willfully misclassifying workers as independent contractors, plus certification and notification requirements on every bid. Firms that misclassified to cut labor costs would lose that advantage; compliant firms faced paperwork.

industries.industry: Employers using large part-time and temporary workforces (retail, fast food, services)
industries.note: Would have had to pay part-timers the same as full-timers for equal work, extend health and pension coverage, and cover them in WARN layoffs. Workers in these jobs were often underpaid relative to full-timers, so the employer cost was the worker's gain.

industries.industry: Employers misclassifying employees as independent contractors
industries.note: The safe harbor that let businesses treat workers as non-employees was narrowed, and state unemployment systems would have had to cover more workers. Much of the payroll-tax and benefit savings from misclassification would have ended.

industries.industry: Pension and group health plan administrators
industries.note: New rules on part-time participation, vesting, health premiums, and portable pension accounts would have added compliance work, though the bill gave collectively bargained plans extra lead time.
